To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the time scale of rapid lake drainage depends on the temperature of ice below the lake, and 2) the temperature dependence of the time scale is explained by the opening of crevasse systems by slow creep.

the time evolution of the 2006 Greenland lake drainage event was controlled by the opening of a pre-existing crevasse system, and that the opening of such a system by slow creep is strongly dependent on the average temperature of ice beneath the lake.

(i) rapid drainage of supraglacial meltwater into the bed of the ice sheet occurs on a time scale that depends strongly on the temperature of ice beneath the lake and (ii) the time scale of the drainage event is consistent with observations of the 2006 event.

a supraglacier lake, of a size of 44×10^{6} m^{3}, can drain into a pre-existing crevasse system, which has opened up by slow creep, and can do so on a time scale of 1 hr or less if the temperature of the ice is at least 5–7 °C below melting point.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a hydraulic fracture, which is the main mechanism of the drainage, can nucleate and propagate at a time that is comparable to the time scale of a lake drainage event.
the time scale for rapid drainage into the ice sheet is determined by a combination of slow creep and rapid hydraulic fracturing.

, in the case of a supragalcial lake draining through a pre-existing crevasse system to a hydraulic fracture on the bed, the time scale for the drainage event is strongly controlled by the slow creep opening and subsequent hydraulic fracturing of the crevasce system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rapid drainage of such a lake into a crevasse is a natural phenomenon, and it is not necessary to invoke a sudden, rapid opening of the crevasses to account for the observed time scale.
a pre-existing, slowly opening crevasse system can provide a pathway for rapid drainage, even if the hydraulic fracture is nucleated at a relatively high pressure.
such a drainage event can be modeled by a combination of slow creep and rapid fracture, both of which can be estimated from the ice sheet’s thermal structure.
